exploration.title: Sound Playground
exploration.subject: Physics
exploration.summary: Change a string’s length, tension and vibration size to investigate pitch and energy.
exploration.question: Why can two plucks sound equally high but have different strengths?
exploration.explanation: A vibrating string can make the air vibrate, producing sound. Frequency counts vibrations per second and helps determine pitch. A shorter string or greater tension produces a higher frequency when the string’s mass per length stays fixed. Amplitude is the size of a vibration; increasing it adds energy without changing this model’s pitch. The model shows an ideal string’s lowest vibration pattern, not every vibration in a real instrument. The drawing slows or stops the motion so you can inspect the string’s shape.

experiments.title: Shorten the string
experiments.instruction: Keep tension and amplitude fixed. Predict what happens to frequency when you halve the string length, then compare the readings at each length.
experiments.observe: Compare the frequency readings: halving the length doubles the frequency here. Explain how that changes pitch.

experiments.title: Change the pluck, not the pitch
experiments.instruction: Keep length and tension fixed. Predict whether a larger amplitude changes frequency, then compare two amplitude settings.
experiments.observe: The vibration gets larger and its energy increases while frequency stays the same. Explain the difference between vibration size and vibration rate.

exploration.misconception: A larger vibration is not the same as a higher pitch. Pitch depends mainly on frequency, not amplitude.
